items.readable_text:
Content:
It is often more convenient to use polar coordinates to determine the points of intersection of two curves. This is especially true if we are dealing with two circles.

Content:
Suppose, for example, that we are given the circles [MATH: {\color{}r=\sqrt2\, {\sin{\theta}}}\,] and [MATH: \, {\color{}r=1},] as shown in the figure below. How do we determine the polar coordinates of the points of intersection of these two curves?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5cf7e0979e65c75651879c62539e3533]

Content:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we must solve the following system of equations for [MATH: r] and [MATH: \theta\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {r = sqrt(2)\sin θ; r = 1]
So, we begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for [MATH: \theta.] This gives

Content:
[MATH: sqrt(2)\sin θ|= 1; \sin θ|= (1)/(sqrt(2)); = (sqrt(2))/(2).]

Content:
Solving this equation in the interval [MATH: [0,2\pi),] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \qquad \theta_2 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.]

Content:
Also, notice that [MATH: r=1] at both intersection points. Therefore, the polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

Content:
[MATH: (r,\theta)=\bigg(1, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\bigg)\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad(r,\theta)=\bigg(1, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\bigg).]

sections.normalized_html:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for [MATH: r] and [MATH: \theta\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: {r = − 4\cos θ; r = 2] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for [MATH: \theta.] This gives

[MATH: − 4\cos θ|= 2; \cos θ|= − (1)/(2).]

Solving this equation in the interval [MATH: [0,360^\circ),] we obtain [MATH: \theta =120^\circ] and [MATH: \theta = 240^\circ.]

Also, notice that [MATH: r=2] at both intersection points.

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the point [MATH: B] are [MATH: (r,\theta)=\big(2, \, 240^\circ\big).]

The circles [MATH: r=4\cos \theta] and [MATH: r=4\sqrt{3}\sin \theta] intersect at points [MATH: O] and [MATH: A,] as shown in the diagram. What are the polar coordinates of the point [MATH: A?]

[IMG: /graphics/37792366bd169f0d2d8644df583be12a]

sections.normalized_html:
First of all, we notice from the graph that [MATH: (r,\theta)=\left(0, 0\right)] is an obvious first point of intersection.

To find the second point of intersection, we set the equations of the curves equal to each other and solve for [MATH: \theta\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 4sqrt(3)\sin θ|= 4\cos θ; (\sin θ)/(\cos θ)|= (4)/(4sqrt(3)); \tan θ|= (1)/(sqrt(3))]

This gives us the solution [MATH: \theta =\dfrac{\pi}{6}] in the [MATH: 1]st quadrant.

Now, we use the equation [MATH: r=4\cos \theta] to find the [MATH: r]-coordinate of the point [MATH: A\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r|= 4\cos ((π)/(6)); = 4 ⋅ (sqrt(3))/(2); = 2sqrt(3)]

Therefore, polar coordinates of the point [MATH: A] are [MATH: (r,\theta)=\left(2\sqrt{3}, \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right).]
